hero.name: Sameer
hero.who: a 31-year-old purchase manager at a Surat textile mill who decides everything in a hurry

story.b: Sameer is proud of being quick. At the textile mill in Surat, suppliers start calling him at eight, and he decides in seconds. Yes to the dye order. No to the new cotton trader. Yes to the cheaper thread. On Friday the cheaper thread snaps on three looms, and the floor supervisor stands at his desk holding a tangled spool. The same evening Sameer realises he booked a family trip to Udaipur in a flash sale without checking the dates of his niece's board exams. His wife asks what he was thinking. Sitting on the mill terrace with a cold cutting chai, he honestly cannot say. Every one of those choices felt obviously right at the time, and that is what bothers him most.

ask.q: Sameer cannot explain his own choices this week. What is the most useful first step for him?
o: Blame the thread supplier and move on
Look back at the week and notice which choices he made without really thinking
Promise himself he will never decide anything quickly again
ask.why: Blaming the supplier hides the pattern, and banning quick decisions is impossible for someone who makes fifty a day. Simply noticing which choices were rushed is the first step, because he cannot fix a habit of mind he has not yet seen.

chapters.take: You cannot fix rushed thinking until you notice when it happens.

story.b: Sameer starts a small test. Before each decision, he asks himself one question: is this a fast one or a slow one? Which truck goes to the Ring Road market is fast, and he lets his gut decide. Then a cotton trader calls with a huge discount, but only if Sameer pays in advance by evening. His gut says grab it. This time he marks it slow. He asks for the trader's papers, calls two mill owners he trusts, and looks up the firm's registration. It turns out the firm is only five weeks old and nobody has heard of it. Sameer politely says no. By lunch he has made forty fast decisions and one slow one, and the slow one may have saved the mill a lot of money.

ask.q: A stranger offers a big one-day discount if Sameer pays in advance. What should he do?
o: Treat it as a slow decision and check the trader's record before paying anything
Grab it quickly, since his instinct says the deal is good
Bargain for an even bigger discount and then pay
ask.why: An urgent offer from a stranger is exactly where fast thinking slips, because the deadline is designed to stop careful thought. Bargaining harder still assumes the deal is real. Slowing down to check costs a few hours and could save a large advance.

chapters.take: When a choice is new, costly or rushed, switch to slow thinking.

story.b: Every March, a dye salesman visits for the yearly contract. Last year he opened at four hundred rupees a kilo, and settling at three hundred and forty felt like a victory. This year, the night before the meeting, Sameer spreads out his old invoices on the dining table. He calls a supplier in Ankleshwar for a rough rate and checks what two other mills pay. He decides that three hundred is fair. In the meeting he speaks first and names his figure calmly. The salesman frowns, talks about rising costs, and they settle at three hundred and fifteen. Driving home past the Tapi bridge, Sameer realises how much last year's first number had quietly shaped what he thought was a good deal.

ask.q: Sameer's junior is negotiating a transport contract next week. What advice fits best?
o: Let the transporter quote first, then bargain hard from there
Avoid naming any number so he does not look cheap
Research fair rates and state a reasonable number of his own early
ask.why: Whoever names the first number sets the anchor, and every later offer gets pulled toward it. Letting the transporter go first hands him that power, and staying vague changes nothing. Researching fair rates and opening with a sensible figure makes the anchor work for him instead.

chapters.take: The first number sticks. Decide yours before you hear theirs.

story.h: The car he would not sell
story.b: Sameer's old hatchback has visited the garage near Udhna four times since Diwali. Each time he pays the bill and tells himself it is fixed now. His mechanic friend says plainly that the engine is tired. A colleague offers to buy the car, but for far less than Sameer paid, and the number feels like a slap. One night he sits with a notepad and writes it all down: the repair bills, the morning it would not start and he missed a buyer's visit, the money he would get today. Looking at the page, he sees that the only thing stopping him is the sting of losing money that is already gone. On Sunday he sells the car and starts taking the mill's staff bus.

ask.q: Sameer's sister keeps a shop lease that loses money monthly, because leaving means losing her deposit. What should she ask herself?
o: How to win back the deposit before she leaves
Whether fear of losing the deposit is hiding a clearly better choice
How long she can keep going before deciding anything
ask.why: The deposit feels huge because losses sting more than equal gains please. That feeling can keep her paying every month just to avoid one loss. Asking whether fear is steering her lets her compare honestly, while chasing the deposit or delaying only deepens the hole.

chapters.take: Losses sting extra. Do not let that sting make your choices.

story.b: A new quality checker joins the mill, a quiet young man from Navsari. In his first week he arrives late twice. Sameer feels the label forming at once: careless, not serious, will not last. He is about to mention it to the owner. Then he stops and asks himself what he does not know yet. He calls the young man in, offers him tea, and asks. The first bus from Navsari is always late, and he has to change buses at the station. Sameer also learns, from the floor supervisor, that this same checker caught a faulty batch that two seniors had missed. Sameer moves his start time by twenty minutes. Walking back to his desk, he wonders how often he has judged people from one scene.

ask.q: A buyer's manager sends Sameer a curt one-line email. What is the wisest response?
o: Ask himself what he might not know, and call the manager to check
Reply equally curtly so the buyer knows the mill has standards
Decide the buyer is unhappy and offer a discount at once
ask.why: One short email gives his mind very little to go on, yet it will happily build a whole story. A curt reply or a panicked discount both act on that invented story. A quick call fills in the missing facts, and often the person was simply busy.

chapters.take: Feeling sure is not the same as being right. Ask what is missing.

story.b: The family trip to Udaipur, now moved to the right dates, comes up in December. Sameer remembers their last holiday to Saputara. It was mostly lovely, but it ended with a six-hour jam on the ghat road, a carsick nephew and everyone snapping. Now the whole family calls it the bad trip. This time Sameer plans the ending as carefully as the beginning. The last evening is a boat ride on the lake at sunset and dinner at a rooftop place his cousin recommended. They leave early the next morning to beat the traffic, with a tiffin of theplas and a playlist the kids chose. Weeks later, whenever someone mentions Udaipur, the children talk about the boat and the lights on the water.

ask.q: Sameer is planning the mill's yearly staff dinner. Where should he put his effort so people remember it well?
o: Spread the budget evenly across every part of the evening
Spend most on a grand welcome, since first impressions matter most
Make sure the best moment and the ending are warm, like sweets and thanks at the gate
ask.why: People mostly remember the strongest moment and how things ended, not the average of every minute. A grand welcome fades if the night ends in a messy rush, and spreading money evenly misses the moments memory keeps. A warm high point and a kind ending shape the memory.

chapters.take: People remember the best moment and the ending. Plan both with care.

story.b: Sameer is still quick. He still decides which truck goes where without a second thought, and the suppliers still call at eight. But a few small things have changed. When an offer is new, costly or rushed, he writes slow on a sticky note and sleeps on it. Before any negotiation he decides his own number the night before. When someone annoys him, he asks himself what he might not know. The quality checker from Navsari now trains two new staff. The mill's staff dinner ended with jalebis at the gate, and people still talk about it. His wife teases him that he takes longer to choose a restaurant now. Sameer laughs. He has not regretted a big decision in weeks.

chapters.take: Think fast on small things, slow on big ones, and learn to tell them apart.
